column6: Generator — one convenient way to make an iterator; iterable-vs-iterator is the general contract.

column3: A bard who freezes mid-sentence the instant he hands you a verse — statue-still, wine glass raised — and thaws exactly there when you tap his shoulder for the next line.
column4: A function containing yield: calling it returns a generator, and each next() resumes the body until the next yield, pausing in place.
column5: def countdown(n): / while n: yield n; n -= 1 / list(countdown(3)) # [3, 2, 1]
column6: return — ends the function forever with one value; yield emits one value and suspends, keeping locals alive.

column3: The list comprehension prints the entire phone book; the genexp is the same clerk who whispers you one number each time you lean in — the building never fills with paper.
column4: Comprehension syntax in parentheses producing a lazy generator instead of a list in memory: (f(x) for x in xs).
column5: sum(x*x for x in range(10**8)) # tiny memory / [x*x for x in range(10**8)] # gigabytes
column6: List comprehension — brackets, materializes everything now; a genexp computes items on demand, once.

column3: A scarf knitting itself off the needles forever; grandma just scissors off two meters when winter comes. The rest exists only as intention.
column4: Laziness lets you define endless streams — counters, cycles, primes — and take only what you need with islice or takewhile.
column5: from itertools import count, islice / evens = (n for n in count() if n % 2 == 0) / list(islice(evens, 5)) # [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]
column6: Infinite loop bug — spins without yielding control; an infinite generator politely pauses between items.

column3: An IV drip through three inline filters: one drop travels the entire line before the next drop leaves the bag — no bucket ever fills between stages.
column4: Chain generators so each item flows through every stage one at a time — constant-memory streaming over data of any size.
column5: lines = open('huge.log') / errs = (l for l in lines if 'ERROR' in l) / first = islice((l.upper() for l in errs), 10)
column6: Chained list map/filter — each stage builds a full list; generator stages hold one item at a time.

column3: A sparkler: dazzling as it burns down the wire, then a dead gray stick — wave it again and there is no error, just no light.
column4: An iterator or generator can be consumed only once; after the pass it stays empty, and re-looping silently yields nothing.
column5: g = (x for x in [1, 2, 3]) / sum(g) # 6 / sum(g) # 0 — silently empty!
column6: List re-iteration — lists restart fresh on every loop; a generator keeps its spent cursor forever.

column3: A plumber's belt of odd brass fittings: one splices two streams into one (chain), one cuts a viewing window (islice), one loops a hose back into itself (cycle).
column4: Python's standard kit of lazy iterator combinators — count, cycle, chain, islice, takewhile, groupby — for composing streams.
column5: from itertools import chain, islice, cycle / list(islice(cycle('AB'), 5)) # A B A B A / list(chain([1, 2], [3])) # [1, 2, 3]
column6: functools — tools acting on functions (partial, reduce, lru_cache); itertools acts on iterators.

column3: A mousetrap holding a computation: nothing whatsoever happens until you poke it and it goes THUNK — then, and only then, the cheese math springs.
column4: A zero-argument function wrapping an expression to delay its evaluation; calling the thunk forces the value — laziness by hand.
column5: thunk = lambda: expensive(42) / # ...later, only if needed: / value = thunk()
column6: Promise/Future — represents work already started elsewhere; a thunk starts no work until called.

column3: Algebra class taught with food: a combo meal is pizza AND soda (product); the daily special is pizza OR pasta OR soup (sum). Menus are algebra.
column4: A type built by combining others two ways: AND (product: this field and that) or OR (sum: this variant or that).
column5: type Shape = Circle(r) | Rect(w, h) # a sum of products
column6: Abstract data type (also ADT) — an interface hiding implementation; algebraic types are about value shape.

column3: A bento box with every compartment filled at once — rice AND fish AND pickles. The menu multiplies: 3 rices times 4 fishes is 12 possible boxes.
column4: A type whose values hold one of each field simultaneously — tuples, records, structs; its value count is the product of field counts.
column5: Point = namedtuple('Point', 'x y') / p = Point(3, 4) # has both fields, always
column6: Sum type — holds exactly one variant at a time; a product holds all fields at once.

column3: A railroad switch: the train sits on exactly one track at any moment, and the big lever's tag tells you which — never straddling two rails.
column4: A type whose value is exactly one of several tagged variants — enums with payloads, tagged unions; value count is the sum of the variants'.
column5: enum Shape { Circle(f64), Square(f64) } // Rust / let s = Shape::Circle(2.0);
column6: Untagged C union — the same memory trick without the tag, so you cannot safely ask which variant is live.

column3: A chocolate orange: one sharp twist and it falls apart into labeled segments that land in your named, cupped fingers.
column4: Binding names to pieces of a structure in one pattern-shaped assignment — unpacking tuples, dicts, or objects by their shape.
column5: x, y = (3, 4) / first, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4] / const {id, ...extra} = row; // JS
column6: Pattern matching — destructuring plus conditional dispatch; destructuring alone assumes the shape fits.

column3: A coin sorter with shaped slots: each falling value tumbles past star, square, and circle holes and drops through the first hole shaped like itself, into that arm's bucket.
column4: A control structure that tests a value against shape patterns, binds their pieces, and runs the first matching arm.
column5: match cmd: / case ('move', x, y): go(x, y) / case ('quit',): bye()
column6: switch/case — compares equality against constants; match tests nested structure and binds variables.

column3: The nightclub bouncer checks your outfit (pattern) AND scans your ID under UV light (guard); dressed right with a fake ID, you fall through to the next bouncer down the line.
column4: An extra boolean condition on a match arm — case pattern if test — so the arm needs both the shape and a truth to fire.
column5: match point: / case (x, y) if x == y: print('diagonal') / case (x, y): print('off-diagonal')
column6: Nested if inside the arm — runs after committing to the arm; a failed guard falls through to later arms.

column3: A joker card at the bottom of the deck that impersonates any card slapped onto it, but has amnesia — it never remembers what it matched.
column4: The catch-all pattern (_ in most languages) that matches anything without binding a name — the match's final safety net.
column5: match code: / case 200: ok() / case _: raise Unknown(code)
column6: Named catch-all (case x) — also matches everything but binds the value; _ deliberately discards it.

column3: A pre-flight clipboard that refuses takeoff until every seat is ticked; bolt a new row onto the plane and every old clipboard in the fleet starts flashing red.
column4: The compiler proves your match handles every variant of a sum type, so each newly added variant turns unfixed matches into errors.
column5: // Rust / match light { Red => stop(), Green => go() } / // error: non-exhaustive — Yellow not covered
column6: Default arm — silences the checker forever; exhaustiveness is compile-time proof precisely because there is no default.

column3: A one-way turnstile forged so its gears physically cannot spin backwards: no 'do not enter' sign needed — the wrong motion does not exist in the machine.
column4: Design types so invalid combinations simply cannot be constructed — the type system, not runtime checks, excludes nonsense.
column5: # bad: is_loading, data, error can conflict / # good: / State = Loading | Loaded(data) | Failed(err)
column6: Validation — rejects bad values at runtime borders; this removes the bad values from the type universe.

column3: Identical white pills repackaged into loudly labeled bottles — ASPIRIN vs RAT POISON: the pharmacist physically cannot pour one bottle against the other's prescription.
column4: Wrap a primitive in a distinct zero-cost type — UserId(int), Meters(float) — so the compiler stops you mixing semantically different values.
column5: struct Meters(f64); struct Feet(f64); / fn climb(h: Meters) { ... } / climb(Feet(3.0)) // compile error
column6: Type alias — just a nickname the compiler sees through; a newtype is a genuinely distinct type.

column3: Instead of the kitchen shrieking a fire alarm through the whole restaurant, the waiter lays a small red card on your table: 'no fish today' — you must pick it up to see the plate beneath.
column4: Return failures as ordinary data the caller must handle, instead of throwing exceptions that teleport control up the stack.
column5: val, err := parse(s) // Go / if err != nil { return nil, err }
column6: Exceptions — nonlocal control flow invisible in signatures; error values appear right in the return type.

column3: A ring box that might be empty: the box's very shape forces you to open it and look before proposing — you cannot slide an unopened box onto a finger.
column4: A container holding either one value (Some/Just) or nothing (None/Nothing), forcing callers to acknowledge absence in the type.
column5: def find(uid) -> Optional[User]: ... / u = find(7) / if u is not None: greet(u)
column6: null — an unmarked landmine any reference may hide; Option marks possible absence in the type and demands unwrapping.

column3: An exam envelope containing either a diploma or a red-inked page listing exactly which questions you failed — never both, never empty.
column4: A container holding success (Ok/Right) or failure with a reason (Err/Left) — like Option, but the empty case carries an explanation.
column5: fn parse(s: &str) -> Result<i32, ParseError> / match parse(x) { Ok(n) => use_it(n), Err(e) => log(e) }
column6: Option — models absence with no reason attached; Result's failure branch carries the error details.

column3: A lab glovebox: your bare hands work on whatever sits inside through sealed rubber gloves — and if the chamber is empty, your hands just wave in the void, no harm done.
column4: Apply a plain function inside the container without opening it: Some(2).map(sq) is Some(4); None and Err pass through untouched.
column5: found.map(lambda u: u.email) # Option stays Option / Ok(2).map(sq) # Ok(4) / Err(e).map(sq) # Err(e), untouched
column6: flatMap — for functions that themselves return a container; plain map would double-wrap their result.

column3: The matryoshka customs desk: each checkpoint tries to slip your doll inside another doll, but the officer instantly cracks the outer shell so you always walk on carrying exactly one doll.
column4: Chain a container-returning function without nesting: flatMap flattens one layer so Option-of-Option never forms; also called bind or and_then.
column5: user.flatMap(get_cart).flatMap(checkout) / # with plain map: Some(Some(Some(...))) nesting
column6: map — lifts a plain-value function; reach for flatMap when the function returns Some/Ok itself.

column3: A FUN-house mirror hall: whoever walks through gets transformed head to toe, but the hall itself — doors, length, lighting — never changes shape.
column4: Any context you can map over while preserving its structure — lists, Option, Result, promises — obeying identity and composition laws.
column5: [1, 2, 3] mapped with sq -> [1, 4, 9] # same length / Some(2) mapped with sq -> Some(4) # same shape
column6: Monad — a functor that also has flatten/bind for chaining; every monad is a functor, not vice versa.

column3: Two sealed test tubes clicked into a mixing machine — one holds a chemical, the other a recipe slip — and the machine combines them without ever unsealing either tube on the bench.
column4: A functor that can also wrap plain values (pure) and apply a wrapped function to a wrapped value, combining independent contexts.
column5: -- Haskell validation / User <$> okName <*> okAge / -- both checked; failures can accumulate
column6: Monad — sequences dependent steps where the next needs the previous result; applicative combines independent ones.

column3: A subway line where every station might eject you: one swipe (bind) carries you station to station, and if any gate slams you leave the whole line — the track itself handles the plumbing between stops.
column4: A context with wrap (unit) and chain (bind), letting context-returning steps sequence cleanly — a programmable semicolon.
column5: Some(u).flatMap(cart).flatMap(pay).flatMap(receipt) / # any None short-circuits the whole chain
column6: Functor/applicative — weaker powers; only a monad lets one step's output decide the next step's context.

column3: A model train on twin rails: the green rail runs through every station's machinery; at the first jam a switch shunts the train onto the red rail, which glides past all remaining stations straight to the report desk.
column4: Model a workflow as a two-track railway: data speeds down the success track and any failure switches it to a parallel error track that bypasses the rest.
column5: result = (validate(inp) / .and_then(save) / .and_then(notify)) # an Err skips ahead
column6: try/except around everything — one catch-all jump; ROP threads the failure through typed returns step by step.

column3: Opening the maybe-empty ring box at the altar: unwrap_or slips a backup candy ring from your pocket; bare unwrap faints in front of everyone if the box is empty.
column4: Boundary escape hatches: getOrElse/unwrap_or supply a fallback value, while bare unwrap asserts success and crashes on the empty case.
column5: port = cfg_port.unwrap_or(8080) / val = opt.unwrap() # panics if None / x = d.get('k', 0) # dict default
column6: flatMap chaining — stays inside the container's safety; unwrap ends it and returns to plain values.

column3: Two airlines: Static Air x-rays every bag at check-in so bad bags never board; Dynamic Air opens bags mid-flight, and some explode over the ocean.
column4: Static: types checked before the program runs, via annotations or inference; dynamic: values carry types and checks happen mid-run.
column5: let n: number = 'hi' // TS: compile error / n = 'hi'; n + 5 # Python: TypeError at runtime
column6: Strong vs weak — how strictly types coerce, an independent axis; Python is dynamic AND strong.

column3: Two blenders: the strong one jams and beeps when a fork falls into the smoothie; the weak one cheerfully liquefies the fork and serves it to you.
column4: Strong: operations on mismatched types fail loudly; weak: the language silently coerces — '5' + 3 errors in Python, yields '53' in JS.
column5: '5' + 3 # Python: TypeError (strong) / '5' + 3 // JS: '53' (weak coercion)
column6: Static vs dynamic — when checks happen; strong/weak is how strict conversions are. JS is dynamic AND weak.

column3: A tiny Sherlock living in your margins: from a single ash flake — the literal 5 — he writes 'integer' in his notebook and shadows that variable through the whole file, deducing every step.
column4: The compiler deduces types from usage so you get full static safety without writing annotations — let n = 5 is known to be an int.
column5: let xs = vec![1, 2, 3]; // Rust infers Vec<i32> / val s = "hi" // Kotlin infers String
column6: Dynamic typing — no compile-time types at all; inference is static typing, just written for you.

column3: A cookie cutter stamped <T> forged from memory-metal: press it into dough, clay, or snow and it becomes a dough-cutter, clay-cutter, snow-cutter — never mixing crumbs between them.
column4: Write code once over a type parameter T and use it at many concrete types with full type safety — parametric polymorphism.
column5: def first(xs: list[T]) -> T: return xs[0] / Box<int> and Box<str> share one Box<T> code
column6: Any/object — also fits everything but erases type info; generics preserve the link between input and output types.

column3: A duck-call contest judged blindfolded: a robot, a comedian, and an actual duck all advance, because the judge only ever listens for the quack().
column4: Dynamic-language polymorphism: any object with the right methods works, checked only at the call — if it quacks, it's a duck.
column5: def feed(a): a.quack() / feed(Duck()); feed(RobotDuck()) # both fine / feed(Cat()) # AttributeError at runtime
column6: Structural typing — the same shape-based idea verified statically at compile time; duck typing fails at runtime.

column3: A locksmith checks keys by holding them against a traced silhouette: any key with the same teeth opens the door — nobody asks which factory forged it.
column4: Compatibility by shape: a value satisfies a type if it has the required members, no declaration needed — checked statically (TypeScript, Go).
column5: interface Named { name: string } / const p = { name: 'Ann', age: 3 } / greet(p) // TS: OK, the shape fits
column6: Nominal typing — requires the declared name or lineage; structural inspects only members. Duck typing is its runtime cousin.

column3: A pedigree dog show: your mutt may look identical to the champion poodle, but no papers, no entry — the judge reads bloodline certificates, never fur.
column4: Compatibility by declared name and lineage: identically shaped types stay distinct unless one explicitly declares the relationship (Java, C#).
column5: class Meters { double v; } / class Feet { double v; } / // Java: not interchangeable despite same shape
column6: Structural typing — same shape means compatible; nominal demands the explicit name or inheritance link.

column3: A cat cafe with two chutes: the OUT chute hands you cats, so a cat-dispenser counts as an animal-dispenser (covariant); the IN chute takes food, where an any-animal feeder serves the cats fine — the arrow flips (contravariant).
column4: How subtyping flows through generics: covariant preserves direction (producers/outputs), contravariant flips it (consumers/inputs), invariant allows neither.
column5: Iterable[Cat] -> Iterable[Animal] # covariant / Handler[Animal] -> Handler[Cat] # contravariant / list[Cat] is NOT list[Animal] # invariant
column6: Plain subtyping — Cat vs Animal; variance asks whether Box[Cat] relates to Box[Animal] at all.

column3: Renovating a dark house one room at a time: each rewired room gets bright inspection lighting while the rest stays candlelit but livable — you never have to move out.
column4: Mix dynamic and static code in one program, adding annotations incrementally; unannotated parts stay dynamic (TypeScript, Python + mypy).
column5: def area(r: float) -> float: ... # checked / def legacy(x): ... # still dynamic, coexists
column6: Hints without a checker — decorative comments in effect; gradual typing actually enforces the annotated parts.

column3: Three actors each play 'the doctor' for one night: a mime who fits any script unchanged (parametric), a quick-change artist with a costume per audience (ad-hoc), and the understudy dynasty inheriting the role (subtype).
column4: One interface, many types, three routes: parametric (generics), ad-hoc (overloading/typeclasses), and subtype (inheritance/interfaces).
column5: first(xs) # parametric: works for any T / 1 + 1; 'a' + 'b' # ad-hoc: + overloaded per type / animal.speak() # subtype dispatch
column6: Overloading vs overriding — overloading is ad-hoc, resolved by argument types; overriding powers subtype dispatch.
